response.title: How Nurtura uses your information
summary: Nurtura is a student project at Strathmore University. It gives activity ideas, not medical advice.

Administrators see ratings and comments, never your child's name or your email.

sections.heading: About Nurtura
sections.body: Nurtura is a student project at Strathmore University. It suggests everyday activities to support a young child's development, from pregnancy to 3 years. It gives ideas, not medical advice: it doesn't diagnose anything or replace a health worker.

sections.heading: What we keep
sections.body: Your account: your email address, your password (stored only in a scrambled form that can't be read back) and whether you're a caregiver. If you sign in with Google, only your email is kept. For each child: the name you give (a nickname is fine), their date of birth or due date, their interests and the areas you'd like support with. Also the milestones you record, the activities suggested and why, and whether you marked them done, with any rating or comment. For signing in: one-time codes and the phones you chose to trust, stored only in scrambled form.

sections.heading: Why we keep it
sections.body: Only to suggest activities that fit your child, explain why each one was suggested and show your child's progress. Ratings and comments help us see which activities work. We don't sell your information, show adverts or use it for anything else.

sections.heading: Who can see it
sections.body: You. Nurtura's administrators can read ratings and comments to review activities, but without your child's name or your email. Sign-in codes reach you through an email service.

sections.heading: On your phone
sections.body: So the app works offline, it keeps your children's list and their latest suggestions on your phone. They are removed when you log out or delete your account.

sections.heading: How long we keep it
sections.body: Until you delete it. You can delete a child's profile, or your whole account, at any time from the Family tab. Deleting is immediate and can't be undone: everything linked to that child or account is removed.

sections.heading: Your child's information
sections.body: Only add a child if you are their parent or guardian, or their parent or guardian has agreed. You can use a nickname instead of their real name.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: Under Kenya's Data Protection Act, 2019, you can ask what we hold about you, correct it (you can edit a child's profile in the app), have it deleted, and withdraw your agreement at any time by deleting your account. If you're unhappy with how your information is handled, you can complain to the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (www.odpc.go.ke).

sections.heading: Changes and questions
sections.body: If this notice changes, the app will ask you to read and agree to the new version. For questions or requests, contact <redacted>.

reasons.source: CDC 2022 checklist / WHO 2006 motor windows (expected age); ASQ-3 scoring convention (Not yet = 0 of 10 points)
reasons.reason: Not yet: “Waves "bye-bye"” — most children do this by 12 months (CDC).
You told us you'd like support with Language development.
Enjoys “water”, which sensory activities build on.

recommendations.description: Talk through daily routines as you do them and make up short songs about them: a washing-hands song, a getting-dressed song. Use the same songs every day so the child learns the words.
recommendations.cultural_relevance: Make up songs in Kiswahili or the mother tongue to familiar tunes.
recommendations.explanation: You recorded “Waves ‘bye-bye’” as not yet; most children do this by 12 months. You said you'd like support with language and communication. It's designed for children aged 12–18 months, your child's age group. Its aim is to help your child learn words for the things you do every day.

recommendations.description: When the child says a word or part of a word, repeat it clearly and add a little more. If they say 'ba', say 'Ball! A red ball!' Keep your words simple, and smile to show you understood them.
recommendations.cultural_relevance: Works in any language spoken at home.

It's designed for children aged 12–18 months, your child's age group. Its aim is to help your child learn new words by building on the ones they say.

recommendations.description: Hold a soft toy and pretend it is talking to the child: 'Hello! What are you eating?' Give the child their own toy and see if they talk back or copy you. Keep the voices playful.
recommendations.cultural_relevance: A homemade cloth doll works as well as a bought one.
recommendations.explanation: You recorded “Waves ‘bye-bye’” as not yet; most children do this by 12 months. You said you'd like support with language and communication. It's designed for children aged 12–18 months, your child's age group. Its aim is to invite your child to talk and pretend with a soft toy.

recommendations.short_description: Float flowers in a shallow container of water. Point to each one and say its colour, then ask the child to point to and pick up a flower.
recommendations.description: Float flowers in a shallow container of water. Point to each one and say its colour, then ask the child to point to and pick up a flower.
recommendations.materials: Wide shallow container; water; flowers or leaves
recommendations.cultural_relevance: Bougainvillea and other garden flowers work well.
recommendations.explanation: You recorded “Waves ‘bye-bye’” as not yet; most children do this by 12 months. You said you'd like support with language and communication. It's designed for children aged 12–18 months, your child's age group. Its aim is to help your child learn colour words while playing with water.

recommendations.short_description: Speak to the child simply using real words rather than baby talk. Give short directions like 'Roll the ball' and show them what you mean.
recommendations.description: Speak to the child simply using real words rather than baby talk. Give short directions like 'Roll the ball' and show them what you mean.
recommendations.cultural_relevance: Use clear words in your home language.
